metadata.note: New Hampshire's own interior rail spine, largely missing from this map before now (the state was previously only touched by through-routes skirting its edges: the Grand Trunk in the far north, the Downeaster/B&M seacoast corridor, and the Vermonter/Montrealer along the Connecticut River border). The Nashua and Lowell Railroad, chartered June 1835 and opened 1838 (18 miles, connecting at Lowell, MA with the Boston and Lowell Railroad), was the first railroad built in New Hampshire. The Concord Railroad, also chartered 1835, completed its Nashua-Concord line (routed through the east bank of the Merrimack at Manchester to serve the Amoskeag Manufacturing Company) by 1842 -- the arrival of the railroad roughly doubled Concord's population within a decade. The Northern Railroad then pushed the line on from Concord to West Lebanon, NH (opening Nov 17 1847, with Daniel Webster speaking at the celebration), reaching the Connecticut River right across from White River Junction, VT -- connecting with the Vermont Central Railroad's own network (see vermont_central_railroad.geojson). Both railroads eventually became part of the Boston and Maine system. This particular corridor (the ex-Concord/Northern route through Manchester and Concord) has had no scheduled passenger service since the 1960s -- but New Hampshire as a whole is NOT without passenger rail today: Amtrak's Downeaster (see amtrak.geojson) calls at Exeter, Durham, and Dover on its Boston-Brunswick run through the state's seacoast corner, a different corridor entirely from the one modeled in this file. A widely-cited closing date for the B&M's Concord/Manchester-area passenger operations is the last train out of Dover on June 30 1967 (Dover itself later regained service once the Downeaster launched in 2001), used here as an approximate end date for this corridor. GEOMETRY UPGRADED 2026-08-24: replaced the original 5-point hand-placed waypoint approximation with real-traced OpenStreetMap track geometry (Overpass API, shortest-path graph search) -- this corridor is still active today as Pan Am Southern/CSX freight trackage for most of its length. Every hop (Lowell-Nashua-Manchester-Concord-West Lebanon) resolved to a connected, plausible real track path with no straight-line fallbacks needed anywhere on the route.

metadata.not_yet_sourced: Exact year the Concord Railroad and Northern Railroad were formally absorbed into Boston and Maine (both are cited only as 'part of B&M by' a given year, not a precise merger date); whether the June 30 1967 Dover date applies equally to the Concord-Manchester-Nashua-West Lebanon corridor specifically, or whether that segment's passenger service ended earlier or later; frequency for any era, all estimated.
geometry_sources: OpenStreetMap (via Overpass API, overpass.openstreetmap.fr mirror): railway=rail (active) combined with railway=abandoned/disused tagging, Lowell MA to West Lebanon NH; routed via Dijkstra shortest path between each station's geocoded (Nominatim/OSM) coordinates. All hops resolved to connected, plausible paths (distance ratios within ~1.3x of straight-line) with no fallbacks needed.

Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.
